explanations.answer: Yours is the kingdom of God
explanations.explanation: Jesus gives the reason in the same breath: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.” Notice He says yours IS, not yours someday maybe. I once owned nothing but dust, so hearing that makes me want to hug somebody with my mustache. You picked the one He actually said, baker.

Jesus never promises the poor a fat paycheck down the road. The reason He gives is “…for yours is the kingdom of God.” He even turns around a few verses later and says woe to the rich (Luke 6:24). A promise of riches would be a nice thing to hear, but it isn't what's on the page.

Inheriting is a real thing Jesus talks about, just not here. He says the meek will inherit the earth in Matthew 5:5, which is a different line. In this one, the reason for the poor is “…for yours is the kingdom of God.” Easy to mix those two up, baker, they sit close together on the shelf.

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.” Same flip as the hunger line: now it's tears, then it's laughing. I like a promise that ends in laughing, since that's my whole business. Good ear, baker.
Rest sounds lovely, and I'd take a nap right now myself. But Jesus doesn't say rest here. He says the ones who weep now “…will laugh.” The tears get swapped for something loud and happy.
Jesus doesn't say the weepers will forget anything. He says, “…for you will laugh.” It's a flip from weeping to laughing, not a wiped memory. I think that's a sweeter deal anyway.
That's the instruction: “Rejoice in that day and leap for joy…” Leap, baker. Not nod politely, LEAP. I'd try it, but I'd have to take my gold base with me, and that's a whole production.
Hiding is a very human plan, and I respect it. But Jesus doesn't tell them to hide. He says, “Rejoice in that day and leap for joy…” and then gives the reward: “…great is your reward in heaven.”
Jesus never tells them to argue their case here. His words are “Rejoice in that day and leap for joy…” A defense speech and a happy leap are very different moves. The text gives the leap.
True. Jesus says, “…great is your reward in heaven.” That's said to the ones hated because of the Son of Man. Rejoicing has a reason attached, baker, and the reason is big.
It's actually true. Jesus says, “…great is your reward in heaven.” He says it to the ones people hate and reject because of the Son of Man. So the rejoicing comes with a reason attached.

That's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says, “But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort.” Already, baker. Not later, not on layaway. The comfort has been handed over, and that's the problem.
False, and you caught the key word. Jesus says the rich “…have already received your comfort.” The key word is already. He doesn't say later, baker, He says already.

Jesus says, “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.” It's the mirror image of the blessing for the weepers. Laughing now, mourning later, and the other way around for the ones who weep now. You read it right, baker.
Jesus doesn't say anything about being forgotten. He says the ones who laugh now “…will mourn and weep.” The laughing now turns into mourning and weeping.
Friends never come up in this woe. Jesus says, “…for you will mourn and weep.” It's a flip in feelings, from laughing to mourning.

True. Jesus says, “Woe to you when all men speak well of you…” It's the one woe about reputation instead of money or meals. It's a surprising line, since most of us would be thrilled to hear everybody say nice things.
It's true, though it sounds backwards. Jesus says, “Woe to you when all men speak well of you…” Most of us would take a standing ovation any day, me included. But that's the line on the page.

“…for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.” Back in verse 23 the fathers of the haters treated the prophets badly. Here, when all men speak well of someone, the fathers did that for the false prophets. Sharp reading, baker.

Great is a word that shows up in this passage, but it isn't in this spot. Jesus says, “…their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.” The word “great” belongs to the reward in heaven back in verse 23.

No “first” prophets here. Jesus says the fathers treated “…the false prophets…” in the same way, which is the line for when all men speak well of you. Verse 23 is about how the fathers treated the prophets, and this verse is the other side of it.
Jesus says it plain: “Love your enemies…” Not tolerate them, not put up with them. Love. He's talking to the ones who will listen, so I'm all ears and all mustache.
Keeping your distance sounds like a very reasonable plan. But Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you…” The instruction goes toward enemies, not away.
Waiting it out is how I got through the oven's preheat, but that's not what Jesus says about enemies. His words are “Love your enemies…” That's an action, baker, not a waiting game.

“…bless those who curse you…” Bless is the word Jesus picks, baker. Look at the pattern: love your enemies, do good to haters, bless the cursers, pray for the mistreaters. Every one of them is a kind move aimed at someone being unkind.
Avoiding is a normal instinct when somebody curses you. Jesus gives a different word: “…bless those who curse you…” The whole run in these verses is about doing something good for them.
Jesus doesn't say warn here. He says, “…bless those who curse you…” That's the same pattern as “Love your enemies…” and “…do good to those who hate you…” It keeps pointing the same direction.
True. Jesus says, “If someone strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also.” It's a hard one, and He doesn't dress it up. I think this one hurts.

It's true. Jesus says, “If someone strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also.” That's the exact line. It comes right after He says, “…pray for those who mistreat you.” So turning the other cheek is one of His examples of loving your enemies: when someone strikes you, you answer with love instead of striking back.
Jesus actually says the opposite. His words are “…if anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back.” It runs right alongside giving to everyone who asks. I know, baker, it stings a little.
False, and that's right. Jesus says, “…if anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back.” That comes right after “Give to everyone who asks you…” Not an easy teaching, but you read it correctly.

explanations.answer: Do to others as you would have them do to you
explanations.explanation: That's the line: “Do to others as you would have them do to you.” You measure by what you'd want, not by what you got. Short line, baker, and it's all there.

explanations.answer: Treat others the way that they treat you
explanations.explanation: That sounds fair, but it's not what Jesus says. His line starts with what you would have done to you, not what was done to you. Just after this He says even sinners love those who love them (Luke 6:32), so he's asking for more than matching treatment.

explanations.answer: Do good to others when they have earned it
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't put an earning test on this. He says, “Do to others as you would have them do to you.” A little later He says to do good to enemies too (Luke 6:35). Nobody has to qualify first.
True. Jesus says, “Even sinners love those who love them.” He says it right after asking, “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you?” That's the point of the line, baker.
It's true. Jesus says, “Even sinners love those who love them.” He says it right after asking, “If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you?” It's right there in Luke 6:32.

“But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return.” Nothing means nothing. No receipt, no payback, no IOU in the back pocket. That's how you tell it apart from what sinners do.

Interest is the opposite direction. Jesus just said that even sinners lend, “…expecting to be repaid in full.” For enemies, He says to lend “…expecting nothing in return.” No interest, baker, not even a little.

A thank-you would be nice, but Jesus says “…expecting nothing in return.” That includes thanks. In the same verse He says the Most High “…is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.” So the ungrateful get kindness too.

explanations.answer: He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked
explanations.explanation: “for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.” That's what the Most High is like. It's a kindness that doesn't wait to be thanked. You got it, baker.

explanations.answer: He shows kindness only to the faithful
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite. He says the Most High “…is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.” The word only isn't in there. The kindness reaches people who haven't earned it.

explanations.answer: He blesses the ones who bless Him
explanations.explanation: That's a nice-sounding trade, but it's the kind of thing Jesus says sinners do. Remember, even sinners do good to those who do good to them. What He says of the Most High is “…He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.”

explanations.answer: Forgive and you will be forgiven
explanations.explanation: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” It's the third pair after “Do not judge, and you will not be judged.” and “Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned.” Three pairs, same shape. Nice work, baker.

explanations.answer: Pray and you will be heard
explanations.explanation: Praying does show up in this sermon, since Jesus says to pray for those who mistreat you. But He doesn't say it as a pair like this one. The pair after judge and condemn is “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
That one is a real teaching of Jesus, just not in this spot. He says something close to it in Matthew 7:7. The pair that follows judge and condemn here is “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

explanations.answer: The measure you use will be measured back to you
explanations.explanation: “For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.” That's the last reason Jesus gives for giving so freely. Whatever size scoop you carry, that's the scoop coming back. You measured that one right, baker.

explanations.answer: Whatever you hold on to will be taken away
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that here. His reason is “For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.” He's pointing at the measure you give, not at what you keep.

explanations.answer: Your giving will be seen and praised by others
explanations.explanation: Praise from others isn't the reason Jesus gives. He says, “For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.” Nobody mentioned an audience. I'd keep the focus on the measure.
